body:
As commented by @goatchurchprime in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94613 this has a side effect in stereo cases:
* suppose two cameras
  * one camera on the left side of the audio source
  * one camera on the right side of the audio source
  * both cameras are located almost at the same distance from the audio source
* if the **left camera** is a bit closer to the audio source, it will be picked as target with max attenuation by the `AudioStreamPlayer3D` and most sound will be played on the **right speaker** 
* if the **right camera** now moves closer until it is closer than the left camera, the right camera will be picked as target with max attenuation by the `AudioStreamPlayer3D` and most sound will be played on the **left speaker**
* essentially there will be a sharp jump from the left to the right speaker (and vice versa if the cameras stay close)

The idea was to use a `volume_vector` per camera and pick the maximum volume for each channel (left and right) individually. However, in this case setting the pitchscale for the doppler effect is problematic. The pitch scale is associated with the playbacks of the audio stream and not with the camera, so I am not sure how to properly select or mix pitch scales (if this is even possible...?). If the output samples are a mix of multiple cameras, then it is not clear which pitch scale shall be used.

Any ideas here?

Regarding the discussion using the average volume instead of the maximum:
In case you have a single sound source and two cameras. Suppose camera A is very close to the audio source and camera B is far away, almost outside the maximum distance of the audio source. The average volume will be something in middle of the volume of camera A and B, so it will be quieter than A but louder than B (approx. half the volume of A since B is almost out of range). If B now moves outside the maximum distance, the average volume will just be calculated from A, so the overall audio will suddenly increase by approximately factor 2.
IMO this behavior might be even worse than the stereo problem the current solution has. Any opinion on this?

Thanks! I added @kus04e4ek as co author in the commit message :+1:

So I thought you could put `output_volume_vector` on the outside of the loop and keep the maximum values in each of its entries as you loop over the cameras.  You're still keeping one direction of the camera from the loop, so this will still have that flipping from left to right in stereo.

For doppler, you could just keep the fastest or closest moving camera.  It's not an effect that is used very much, in my opinion.  I would guess people would want as much doppler as possible, if it is turned on.  

The reason I don't think doppler is much used is that we don't have the capability of setting a low speed of sound so as to exaggerate its effect.  I wanted to do this in a Augmented Reality application, where you are following a spark moving through the room, and the pitch would tell you if it was coming or going from you.  You have to run pretty quickly to notice anything now with the true speed of sound, and it would be very brief.  If I set the speed of sound down to 10m/s then it could come out pretty nice.

In any case, doppler is improperly implemented.  To do it properly there should be a sound buffer for each source and listener to add a delay based on the distance between them.  Then doppler effect is then simply the result of adjusting the length of this buffer as you move closer and further.  And so with two listeners you would get a double sound like an echo where these delay buffers didn't match.  People would probably almost always interpret it as an echo rather than ears being in different places, which means we probably shouldn't do it that way.

@goatchurchprime  Thanks for the input :+1:
I changed the code now, such that it will use the maximum volume for each channel (left and right) and frame across all cameras. This is pretty similar to the fix which was done in the the [2D audio player](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/76713). I created two temporary vectors, one for the output and one for the reverb volumes. These vectors are used for the individual per camera calculations. I left these calculations unchanged, so they are the same as before. The individual volumes are then fused together by using the maximum from each channel of each frame (for reverb and regular output).
For the Doppler effect I simply use the maximum pitch scale.
I moved all the code which configures the playback and audio buses outside of the camera loop.

From the chat:

> It all runs completely correctly, except there is an UTTERLY UNEXPLAINED muffling of the jazz sound when the left camera is 1/4 of the way out. This defies any logic whatsoever, since it cannot be possible, there are no filters anywhere. 

I had a look into the playground and I also noticed the muffling sound when the left camera passes a certain distance. Interestingly, when I turn the cameras around (180° around the y-axis) the muffling effect sticks to the left camera, but (obviously) switches the sides on my headphones. So the issues seems to be related to the camera instance itself and not any spatial properties.
Another test showed: If you change the order of the SubViewportContainers in the HBoxContainer (which effectively changes the order of the cameras in the scene tree), this also changes the order in which the cameras are processed in the AudioStreamPlayer3D and then also the muffling effect switches from the left camera to the right camera.
The culprit: The linear attenuation was still set in the loop across all cameras (so the last one in the list defined the value). I updated the PR and the issue is now gone 👍
@BuzzLord I have addressed your comments, could you have another look if the PR is alright now?
@BuzzLord Thanks for the finding! I really missed that one. I fixed your and @AThousandShips findings.

@BuzzLord Thanks for the idea. I was aware that the Doppler effect would not work optimally with multiple viewports, but good catch that I actually changed the behavior in the single camera case.
Your approach with a weighted average sounds alright to me, not sure why the logarithmic scale makes sense but I guess its kind of like logarithmic gamma correction in images (I'm actually more an image than an audio person :smile: ).

Just one note on the averaging approach: This might introduce artifacts when cameras leave the maximum range of a `AudioStreamPlayer3D`. Suppose you have one fast and one slow moving camera within the range of an audio source. The overall pitchscale would be composed by the average of the pitchscales of both cameras. As soon as the fast camera moves out of the range of the audio source, the overall pitchscale will only be computed from the pitchscale of the slow camera. So right in the moment when the fast camera moves out of range there will be a noticeable instant change of the pitchscale.

So, for the weighted average I would suggest to use a distance related weight, e.g.

```
(max_distance - distance) / max_distance
```

What do you think?

> Your approach with a weighted average sounds alright to me, not sure why the logarithmic scale makes sense but I guess its kind of like logarithmic gamma correction in images (I'm actually more an image than an audio person 😄 ).

The way I was thinking about it was, if you have one sound that is one octave up (i.e. 2.0x samples per second as normal) and another sound at one octave down (i.e. 0.5x samples per second), an even blend of the two should be just the 1x normal sample rate.

Those multipliers are what the pitch scale is. If you averaged them in linear space, you get `(2.0 + 0.5) / 2 = 1.25`. If you average them in log space you get `(log2(2.0) + log2(0.5)) / 2 = (1.0 + (-1.0)) / 2 = 0.0`, then when you bring them back to linear value, `pow(2, 0.0) = 1.0`.

@BuzzLord Thanks for the explanation and sorry for the long response time (I have been on a business trip). Makes totally sense to me :+1: I implemented the pitch scale calculation as suggested. It seems to do what it should, but do you have a dedicated project / repo where you tested the Doppler effect?

Here's the test project I made. It has a split screen camera scene, with both subviewports set to _audio listener enable 3D_, and the cameras have doppler enabled. The left view is controlled with WASD, the right view is arrow keys. Move the cameras really far apart along the line the sound is moving on to get a blend of approaching and receding doppler shifts.

[test-multiviewport-audio-gh-114080.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24973357/test-multiviewport-audio-gh-114080.zip)

@BuzzLord Thanks for the input and I agree we should avoid the overhead of allocating and freeing the heap memory every iteration. I played around with [`FixedVector`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/templates/fixed_vector.h) instead of plain C-style arrays, but I would still have to adjust various function signatures. In the end I decided to move the tmp vectors to class members as it seems cleaner in terms of changes and existing interface, but it really is a matter of taste IMO.

I also tested this implementation with your example project. The pitch scale seems to adjust fine for approaching and receding objects :+1: I tried both weighted average with and without logarithmic scale and I subjectively feel like the version without logarithmic scale sounds more natural. What do you think?

> I tried both weighted average with and without logarithmic scale and I subjectively feel like the version without logarithmic scale sounds more natural. What do you think?

I tried it out, and it sounds fine to me with linear blending. I was curious how much they differed in the pitches they produced, so I made a little spreadsheet to graph them, and found there's very little difference between the blend methods (at least until around 50% the speed of sound).

Since the whole Doppler pitch blending is not physically based, as long as there's some blending so the pitch doesn't pop, I don't think it really matters which method is used. So I'd say in the interest of performance, the linear blend would be better.

Attached spreadsheet if anyone is interested.
[doppler_pitch_comparison.xlsx](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25140932/doppler_pitch_comparison.xlsx)

I would leave the output volumes using MAX. It matches what the AudioStreamPlayer2D is doing, and makes the code simpler, IMO (i.e. no extra weighting/normalizing all the values, just a simple max). I feel it's also pretty intuitive: the output volume is just the loudest volume from any of the active listeners.

Alright, I reverted that last change :+1: So the pitch scale is computed by a linear weighted average and the volumes are picked by maximum.
Do think this is now ready to be merged?
@BuzzLord Is there anything else I should do with this PR? If not, can you approve and can we merge it?

@Ivorforce Thanks for your review. I either fixed or commented on all your findings :+1:
For the local vectors I changed from `Vector` to `FixedVector` and allocate them now locally on the stack (their capacity is only `4`), instead of switching to `LocalVector`. If you do not like this change, just let me know and I will revert it and use `LocalVector` class members for the temporaries.
@Ivorforce Thanks again, I fixed all of your findings :+1:

@Ivorforce A note on my latest changes: I had to add a explicit initialization of the C-array `real_t volumes[7]`, because the CI ran into a "possibly uninitialized" warning (treated as error) and blocked the build. I guess my change to `FixedVector` triggered this warning as I had to touch some lines where `volumes` was accessed and so the warning got processed by the CI...?
@Ivorforce Is there anything else I should fix or change in this PR? Or do you think it is ready to merge? What would be the next steps to merge it?
I'm good with the approach and code now. Just need to have a final big picture look and haven't found the time yet. But I'd say it's fair to expect we merge it for 4.7 👍
